title: Wealth Architecture: Who Owns It, How Fast You Can Reach It, and in What Currency
summary: A developer's wealth is not one number. It is a set of assets held in different ownership layers, reachable at different speeds, and denominated in different currencies. Designing those three dimensions on purpose is what keeps a good career from being ended by one bad year.
body:
Net worth tells you how much you have. Wealth architecture tells you whether you can use it: who legally owns each asset, how quickly it can become cash, and whether that cash is in the currency you will need to spend.

Recall

Q. What are the six links in the risk chain from the last phase?

A. Allocation by contract, transfer by insurance and surety, retention in the risk register, resolution through the dispute ladder, proof by records, and challenge by independent review.

Q. What does a red team do?

A. It deliberately attacks a plan, structure or estimate to find how it fails, rather than confirming it. It works only if the team is independent and safe to say no.

Q. What is an order of precedence clause in a construction contract?

A. A clause that ranks the contract documents, such as the agreement, conditions, specifications and drawings, so that when two conflict, the higher-ranked one governs.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Warrick. A developer's wealth has a dangerous shape. Most of it is tied up in projects you cannot sell quickly, owned through companies that lenders have taken security over, often backed by guarantees you signed personally. Meanwhile your life costs real money every month, in a particular currency, whatever the market is doing. Developers rarely fail because they are poor on paper. They fail because, in the one month it mattered, the value was in the wrong place, the wrong form or the wrong currency. This phase is about designing against that. Everything here is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Dimension one: ownership layers

In plain English: everything you own sits in a box, and the box decides who can reach it, who taxes it, and what happens to it when you die.

The professional framing is an ownership layer: the legal level at which an asset is held. Typical layers, in principle, are personal ownership; an operating company that employs people and signs contracts; a holding company that owns shares in project companies; single-purpose project companies that each own one building and carry its loan; and, for some families, trusts in which a trustee holds legal title for beneficiaries. Each layer has a different exposure to creditors, a different tax treatment and a different path on death or incapacity.

The design principle is separation by risk. Assets that carry operating or construction risk sit in layers that can fail without reaching the others. Assets meant to protect your family, such as a home and a long-term reserve, sit away from the layers that sign guarantees and contracts. Separation only works if it is real: separate bank accounts, separate records, contracts signed by the right entity, and no habit of moving money casually between layers. Week 21 showed how a court can disregard a company that is run as an extension of its owner.

Dimension two: liquidity tiers

In plain English: some money you can spend tomorrow, some next year, some only when a building sells.

A liquidity tier groups assets by how quickly and how cheaply they can become spendable cash. A common practitioner habit uses three tiers. Tier 1 is cash and near-cash, available within days with no loss, held for living costs and immediate shocks. Tier 2 is assets that can be turned into cash within months at a modest cost, held for opportunities and larger shocks. Tier 3 is long-term and illiquid capital, such as project equity and land, which may take years to realise and may sell at a heavy discount if you are forced. The tiers and their sizes are a personal design choice, not a standard.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A developer has a net worth of 5,000,000 dollars. On paper that looks secure. Broken into tiers: 300,000 dollars in tier 1, 400,000 dollars in tier 2, and 4,300,000 dollars in tier 3, mostly equity in two projects. Living costs are 15,000 dollars a month, and personal guarantees on one loan could require 1,000,000 dollars if costs overrun. Tier 1 covers 20 months of living, which is comfortable, but tier 1 plus tier 2 covers only 700,000 dollars against a 1,000,000-dollar contingent call. If the call comes, 300,000 dollars has to come from tier 3, and selling project equity under pressure might mean accepting a large discount. The net worth was never the problem. The tier sizes were.

Say that out loud now.

Dimension three: currency reserves

In plain English: keep the money for each bill in the currency the bill is paid in.

A currency reserve is a pool of liquid money held in a specific currency to meet obligations in that currency. If your family spends in one currency, your projects borrow in a second, and your income arrives in a third, a sharp move between them can create a shortfall even when every asset still exists. Week 43 taught currency mismatch for projects; the same logic applies to a household.

Second worked example, hypothetical. A family spends the equivalent of 120,000 dollars a year in currency A. Its tier 1 reserve of 240,000 dollars is held entirely in currency B, which earns slightly more. Currency B then falls 25 percent against currency A in a crisis. The reserve is now worth 180,000 dollars in currency A, covering 18 months instead of 24, and if the crisis also closes the banks for a time, even that may be hard to reach. Matching at least the tier 1 reserve to the spending currency, and holding some of it in an institution outside the country under stress, removes most of that risk. The exact split is a decision for you and a licensed adviser.

How the best do it

Well-run family offices and long-term institutional investors typically separate an operating reserve, sized to known obligations and kept boring, from long-term capital that can take risk and wait. They write the reserve size down in a policy and review it on a schedule, rather than adjusting it by mood. A small developer can copy that: a one-page statement of the three tiers, their target sizes, their currencies and the trigger that requires a top-up.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: each ownership layer is taxed differently, and moving assets between layers can itself be a taxable event; get advice before you move anything. Liability: separation protects only if it is real and in place before any claim. Banking: lenders look at your personal liquidity when you guarantee, and a strong tier 1 and tier 2 improves your terms. Governance: write down who may move money between layers and on what authority. Estate: every layer needs a path on death and incapacity, which Week 8 introduced and the trusts weeks will build. Exit: tier 3 becomes cash only at a sale or refinance, so the exit plan of each project is part of your personal liquidity plan.

Professional sign-off required: licensed financial adviser, on reserve sizing and currency; lawyer and accountant, on ownership layers.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a large net worth with a small tier 1 and tier 2, so that one contingent call forces a sale of project equity at the worst price. The control is a written target for each tier, sized to living costs plus your contingent liabilities, reviewed every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

Counting guaranteed exposure as zero because it has not been called. A guarantee is a liability that has not arrived yet; it belongs in the sizing of tier 1 and tier 2.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught that a cost-overrun guarantee puts a real person behind a finished building. That is where project risk crosses into your personal balance sheet. Today's tiers are sized partly so that if that guarantee is called, you pay it from reserves, not from a fire sale.

Recap

Wealth has three dimensions: ownership layer, liquidity tier and currency. Separate layers by risk, size the tiers to living costs plus contingent calls, and match reserves to the currency of spending. Write it on one page and review it.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the Thai baht in 1997, when debts and reserves were in the wrong currency.
checklist: I can list every asset I own by ownership layer.
I can list every asset by liquidity tier, with realistic time to cash.
I know the currency of each major obligation and of each reserve.
My tier 1 and tier 2 targets include my contingent guarantee exposure.
Assets meant to protect my family sit away from the layers that sign guarantees.
I have a written rule for who may move money between layers.
I review the one-page architecture every quarter.
I will take this plan to a licensed adviser before acting on it.
head: Field checklist
speak: My net worth tells me how much I have. Wealth architecture tells me whether I can use it. It has three dimensions. First, ownership layers: whether each asset is held personally, in an operating company, a holding company, a project company or a trust, which decides who can reach it, how it is taxed and what happens on my death. Second, liquidity tiers: tier 1 is cash I can spend within days, tier 2 can become cash within months at modest cost, tier 3 is project equity and land that takes years and sells at a discount if forced. Third, currency: reserves should match the currency of the bills they pay. A developer worth 5,000,000 dollars on paper with 700,000 in the first two tiers and a 1,000,000-dollar guarantee outstanding is fragile. So I size tiers to my living costs plus my contingent calls, match currencies, write it on one page, and review it with a licensed adviser.
terms: Ownership layer — the legal level at which an asset is held, such as personally, in a company or in a trust.
Liquidity tier — a grouping of assets by how quickly and cheaply they can become spendable cash.
Currency reserve — a pool of liquid money held in a particular currency to meet obligations in that currency.

hostile.q: You are worth 5,000,000 dollars. Why are you worried about a 1,000,000-dollar guarantee?
hostile.a: Because only 700,000 dollars of my wealth can become cash within months; the rest is project equity that would sell at a discount under pressure. A called guarantee would force exactly that sale. So I am rebuilding my first two tiers until they cover my living costs and the realistic guarantee exposure together, before I take on a new commitment.

title: The Thai Baht, 1997: When the Debts and the Reserves Were in the Wrong Currency
summary: Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997 after defending its link to the US dollar, and the currency fell sharply. Companies that had borrowed in dollars to fund property and business in baht saw their debts swell overnight. The lesson for a personal balance sheet is that a currency peg is a promise someone else keeps, until they cannot.
body:
For years, borrowing in dollars to build in baht looked like free money: lower interest and a currency that never moved. The currency did not move because someone was holding it still, and on 2 July 1997 they let go.

Recall

Q. What are the three dimensions of wealth architecture?

A. Ownership layer, liquidity tier and currency.

Q. What does Rule 84 protect against?

A. Treating certificates and sign-offs on life-safety systems as proof without independent verification against what was actually built.

Q. What is a limitation of liability clause?

A. A clause that caps the amount one party can recover from another, often at a figure tied to the contract sum or insurance limits, subject to exceptions such as fraud and whatever the governing law will not allow.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Ford, with Roman beside me for the finance and wealth view. You will live with more than one currency: the one you earn in, the one your family spends in, and the ones your lenders lend in. The Thai crisis is the cleanest real case of what happens when a whole economy forgets that a stable exchange rate is a policy, not a law of nature. The facts here are the widely reported ones; the detail is in the economic histories of the period.

Step 1: Timeline

Through the early and middle 1990s, Thailand grew fast and kept the baht closely tied to the US dollar through a managed arrangement. Foreign money flowed in, much of it short-term borrowing in dollars by banks, finance companies and businesses, and a good share went into property, particularly in Bangkok. By 1996 there were signs of oversupply in property and weakness in finance companies. In 1997 speculators bet against the baht, and the central bank spent heavily to defend it. On 2 July 1997 the government let the baht float. It fell sharply over the following months, losing roughly half its value against the dollar at the worst point. Thailand sought support from the International Monetary Fund later that summer, and the crisis spread to other Asian economies.

Step 2: Key decisions

The key private decision was to borrow in dollars, often short-term, to fund long-term assets that earned baht: buildings, land and businesses whose customers paid in local currency. The key public decision was to defend the peg, using reserves, until the reserves could no longer carry it. Both decisions treated the exchange rate as fixed.

Step 3: Assumptions

Three assumptions sat underneath. That the peg would hold, because it always had. That short-term dollar loans could be rolled over, because lenders always had. That property values and demand would keep rising, because they always had. Notice the shape: each assumption was a description of the recent past, offered as a forecast.

Step 4: Incentives

Dollar borrowing was cheaper than baht borrowing, so a borrower who ignored currency risk looked more profitable than one who paid to remove it. Lenders earned fees on volume. Developers earned on completion and sale. Roman's point: no one in the chain was paid to price the event that ended it, a large devaluation, so the cost of that event appeared on nobody's spreadsheet until it arrived on everybody's.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The warning signs were public. Rising vacant office and residential space in Bangkok. A large current account deficit, meaning the country was relying on foreign money each year. Short-term foreign debt that was large relative to the reserves available to repay it. Weak finance companies. Repeated speculative pressure on the currency before the float. Each one was a reason to reduce dollar debt, extend its term, or hedge it. Many borrowers did none of these.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return for an unhedged borrower was not the float itself. It was every day before the float on which the loan stayed in dollars and short. After the float, hedging was expensive or unavailable, lenders were withdrawing, and assets earning baht could not be sold for enough dollars to repay. Roman's lens: the moment to buy protection is when it looks unnecessary, because that is the only moment it is cheap.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a currency mismatch funded by short-term debt: long-term assets earning one currency, financed by loans repayable in another, on terms that could be withdrawn. The peg hid the mismatch, and the peg was a promise kept by someone else's reserves.

Applying it to a personal balance sheet

Worked example one, hypothetical. You borrow the equivalent of 2,000,000 dollars in currency B to fund a building whose rents are paid in currency A, because currency B loans are 2 percentage points cheaper. Saving: about 40,000 dollars a year in interest. Currency A then falls 40 percent against currency B. Your debt, measured in the currency of your rent, rises from the equivalent of 2,000,000 to roughly 3,330,000, because each unit of rent now buys 40 percent less of currency B. The interest saving over five years, 200,000 dollars, is dwarfed by a 1,330,000-dollar increase in debt. That is the arithmetic the Thai borrowers ran in reverse.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your family's reserve sits in a bank inside the economy under stress, in the local currency. If the currency falls and the bank restricts withdrawals for a time, you have lost value and access at once. A reserve split between the spending currency, held locally for daily use, and a stable currency, held outside the stressed system, keeps both value and access. Week 63 called this keeping reserves outside the system you are exposed to.

Roman's three questions for any foreign-currency debt

Roman here. Before you sign any loan in a currency other than your income, ask three questions and write the answers down. First, what is the largest move in this exchange rate in the past, and what would the same move do to my debt measured in my income currency? Second, if the lender would not roll the loan over, how long would I have and where would the repayment come from? Third, what would a hedge cost today, for the whole term, and is the interest saving still positive after paying for it? If the saving disappears once the hedge is priced, you were never saving money; you were selling insurance to the market without being paid for it. Thai borrowers who asked those questions in 1995 or 1996 would have found the answers uncomfortable, and that discomfort was the information.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a long run of stable exchange rates as evidence that rates are stable. The control is to measure every debt and every reserve in the currency of the income or spending it serves, and to stress each one with a large move before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing a foreign-currency loan for its lower interest rate. The rate difference is visible; the currency risk is not. Compare the interest saving against the cost of a realistic devaluation, not against nothing.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman taught currency mismatch, convertibility and transfer risk for projects. Argentina in 2001 and 2002, studied in earlier weeks, showed a peg breaking and contracts changing. Thailand shows the same failure entering through private balance sheets: the mismatch was not the government's alone; it was in thousands of loan agreements.

Recap

Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997 after defending its link to the dollar. Borrowers with dollar debts and baht income saw debts swell. The root cause was a currency mismatch on short-term money, hidden by a peg. Rule 85 keeps your reserves and debts matched to the currency you will need.

Next: Warrick, on The Money: what it costs to hold liquidity, and what it costs not to.
checklist: I measure each debt in the currency of the income that will repay it.
I stress every foreign-currency debt with a large adverse move before signing.
I compare any interest saving against the cost of a realistic devaluation.
I prefer longer terms to short rollover debt for long-term assets.
My tier 1 reserve is mostly in the currency I spend.
Part of my reserve sits outside any one banking system I depend on.
I treat a fixed exchange rate as a policy that can end, not a fact.
head: Field checklist
speak: Through the 1990s Thailand kept the baht closely tied to the dollar. Banks, finance companies and businesses borrowed in dollars, often short-term, because it was cheaper, and much of the money went into property earning baht. By 1996 property was oversupplied and finance companies were weak. In 1997 speculators attacked the currency, the central bank spent heavily defending it, and on 2 July 1997 the baht was floated. It fell sharply, at worst losing about half its value against the dollar. Borrowers with dollar debts and baht income saw their debts swell overnight. The root cause was a currency mismatch funded by short-term debt, hidden by a peg that was really a promise backed by someone else's reserves. For me, the rule is simple: measure every debt and every reserve in the currency I will need, stress it with a large move before signing, and keep part of my reserve outside the system I depend on.
terms: Currency peg — a government or central bank policy that holds an exchange rate fixed or within a narrow band, which can end when reserves run out.
Current account deficit — a country spending more abroad than it earns, so that it relies on foreign money to fill the gap each year.
Rollover risk — the risk that a short-term loan cannot be renewed on maturity, forcing repayment at a bad moment.

hostile.q: The foreign-currency loan is 2 percentage points cheaper. Why would you pay more?
hostile.a: Because the saving is visible and the risk is not. On a hypothetical 2,000,000-dollar loan, the saving is about 40,000 dollars a year, but a 40 percent fall in my income currency would add over 1,300,000 to the debt in the money my rents are paid in. I borrow in the currency of the income, or I price a hedge and compare honestly.

rule: Rule 85: Never fund a long-term asset with short-term debt in a currency other than the one it earns, and never keep my emergency reserve only in a currency or banking system that the shock I fear could devalue or freeze.

title: The Price of Being Able to Pay: Cash Drag Against the Forced-Sale Discount
summary: Holding liquid reserves costs money, because cash and near-cash earn less than long-term assets. Not holding them costs more, but only on the day you are forced to sell. This lesson puts both costs on one page so the reserve becomes a priced decision rather than a feeling.
body:
Every dollar of reserve costs you a little every year. Every dollar of reserve you do not have can cost you a great deal on one bad day. The reserve is the price of never having to sell at the wrong time.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 85 say?

A. Never fund a long-term asset with short-term debt in a currency other than the one it earns, and never keep the emergency reserve only in a currency or banking system the feared shock could devalue or freeze.

Q. Why is a deductible a retained risk in disguise?

A. Because it applies to each event, so the owner pays the first slice of every loss, and many small events can add up to a large retained cost even when the policy is in place.

Q. What is force majeure?

A. A contract clause that relieves a party from liability, usually for delay or non-performance, when defined events beyond its control occur. Its effect depends entirely on the wording and the governing law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers dislike idle cash, because their training says money should be working. That instinct is right for project capital and wrong for reserves. A reserve's job is not to earn; it is to make sure nothing else you own has to be sold at a discount. If you can price that job, you can size the reserve without arguing with yourself. Everything here is conceptual, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The cost of holding: cash drag

In plain English: money kept safe and reachable usually earns less than money tied up for the long term.

Professionally, the cost of holding liquidity is the difference in expected return between the reserve and what the same money might have earned in long-term assets. Call that difference cash drag. Worked example, hypothetical. You hold a tier 1 and tier 2 reserve of 600,000 dollars. Suppose the reserve earns 3 percent and long-term project equity is expected to earn 12 percent. The drag is 9 percentage points on 600,000 dollars: about 54,000 dollars a year of expected return given up. Over five years, ignoring compounding for simplicity, that is about 270,000 dollars. It feels like a lot. These return figures are illustrative, not forecasts.

Two corrections make the drag smaller than it looks. First, project equity's 12 percent is an expected return with a wide range, and a reserve's 3 percent is close to certain, so you are not comparing like with like. Second, the reserve is what lets you hold your project equity to its planned exit instead of selling early; part of the 12 percent depends on the reserve existing.

The cost of not holding: the forced-sale discount

In plain English: something sold in a hurry sells cheaply.

A forced-sale discount is the gap between what an asset is worth to a patient seller and what a buyer will pay a seller who must close quickly. Illiquid assets, such as a minority stake in a private project or a piece of land, can carry large discounts under pressure, because there are few buyers and they know you need cash. Commercial practice, not a standard, but the direction is reliable.

Worked example, hypothetical. A guarantee is called and you need 400,000 dollars within 60 days. Without a reserve, you sell part of a 2,000,000-dollar project stake. A buyer who knows your position offers 25 percent below fair value. To raise 400,000 dollars, you must sell stake worth about 533,000 dollars at fair value: 400,000 divided by 0.75. You have lost about 133,000 dollars of value in one transaction, plus the future return on the part you sold, plus some control over the project. If this happens once in five years, it costs half of what five years of drag on a 600,000-dollar reserve cost. If the discount is worse, or it happens twice, the reserve was the cheaper choice.

Say that out loud now.

Putting both on one page

The decision is a comparison of an annual, nearly certain cost against an occasional, uncertain one. Write it as a table each year.

ItemHypothetical value
Reserve held, tiers 1 and 2600,000 dollars
Annual cash drag at 9 points54,000 dollars
Largest realistic contingent call400,000 dollars
Forced-sale discount if unfunded, at 25 percentabout 133,000 dollars per event
Living costs covered by tier 1months, written as a number

The table does not give a single right answer. It shows the trade, so the choice is deliberate. A developer with no guarantees and a salaried income can run a smaller reserve; one with large personal guarantees and lumpy income needs a larger one. The person who decides is you, with a licensed adviser.

Reducing drag without reducing safety

Three conceptual levers. One, ladder the reserve: tier 1 in instruments available immediately, tier 2 in ones available within weeks or months, which may earn a little more. Two, use committed but undrawn borrowing capacity as part of tier 2, but only if the lender cannot withdraw it in exactly the conditions you are reserving against, which is rare; Week 45 showed how bridge money disappears in a stressed market. Three, reduce the contingent calls themselves by negotiating caps and burn-offs on guarantees, which shrinks the reserve you need. This lesson names no product; the instruments are a matter for your adviser.

What the lender sees

There is one more benefit to a sized reserve that does not appear in the drag calculation. When you sign a personal guarantee, the lender assesses your liquidity, not only your net worth. A guarantor with 600,000 dollars of verifiable liquid assets against a 400,000-dollar realistic call is a guarantor the lender believes. That can earn better terms: a lower cap, an earlier burn-off, or a smaller equity requirement. The reserve therefore pays a dividend in negotiating power on every project. It is not a return you can book, but it is real, and it shrinks the true cost of the drag.

Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, add a line for contingent liabilities and a line for the reserve that answers them. When the reserve is below the realistic call, your net worth is overstated by the forced-sale discount you would suffer. Write that adjusted figure down; it is the honest one.

Family, legacy and enough

This month's thread is a question only you can answer. Every dollar of reserve is a dollar you have decided does not need to grow, because its job is to protect. At some point, a whole fortune can be thought of that way.

So, Mr Shabazz: what amount of wealth, held safely, would be enough for the life you and your family want, so that everything beyond it is genuinely optional? Write your answer, date it, and expect it to change. Do not let an adviser, a partner or a market define it for you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is cutting the reserve in a good year to fund a new deal, so that the next bad year finds you with a large commitment and no cushion. The control is a written reserve floor that new deals cannot draw on.

The beginner's mistake

Measuring the reserve only against living costs and ignoring guarantees. Living costs are predictable; guarantee calls are what force sales.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick introduced the liquidity floor and asked you to define enough. Today puts prices on the floor: the floor costs cash drag every year and saves a forced-sale discount on the day it is needed. The question of enough is the same question, asked with better numbers.

Recap

Holding a reserve costs cash drag; lacking one costs a forced-sale discount. Put both on one page, size the reserve to living costs plus realistic contingent calls, and protect a written floor from new deals.

Next: Omar, on The Rules: the legal forms of ownership and what each does on death, divorce and a creditor's claim.
checklist: I can state my reserve's annual cash drag in dollars.
I can state the forced-sale discount I would suffer if my largest call came unfunded.
My reserve is sized to living costs plus realistic contingent calls.
I have a written reserve floor that new deals cannot draw on.
I count undrawn credit as reserve only if it cannot be withdrawn in a stressed market.
My balance sheet shows contingent liabilities and an adjusted net worth.
I have written and dated my own answer to what is enough.
head: Field checklist
speak: Holding a reserve costs money. On a hypothetical 600,000-dollar reserve earning 3 percent, while project equity might earn 12, the cash drag is about 54,000 dollars a year. Not holding a reserve also costs money, but on one day. If a guarantee is called for 400,000 dollars and I have no reserve, I may have to sell part of a project stake to a buyer who knows I am forced, at perhaps 25 percent below fair value. Raising 400,000 then means selling stake worth about 533,000, a loss of about 133,000 in one transaction, plus future return and control. So I put both costs on one page every year. I size the reserve to my living costs plus my realistic contingent calls, I protect a written floor that new deals cannot touch, and I show an adjusted net worth when the reserve is short. The decision is mine, with a licensed adviser.
terms: Cash drag — the expected return given up by holding money in safe, liquid form instead of long-term assets.
Forced-sale discount — the gap between an asset's value to a patient seller and the price a buyer pays a seller who must sell quickly.
Contingent liability — an obligation that exists only if a future event happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: Why are you sitting on 600,000 dollars of cash when you could put it into the next project?
hostile.a: Because that cash protects 4,000,000 dollars of project equity from being sold at a discount if a guarantee is called. The drag is about 54,000 dollars a year on hypothetical returns; one forced sale could cost more than twice that. The reserve has a written floor, and new projects are funded from capital above it.

title: How You Hold Title Decides What Happens Next: Ownership Forms and Their Consequences
summary: The same asset behaves differently on death, divorce, a creditor's claim or a sale depending on how it is legally held: in one name, jointly with survivorship, in shares, through a company or by a trustee. This lesson teaches the concepts and how to think about each, with a conceptual comparison of Canada and Guyana.
body:
Two families own identical houses worth the same amount. One passes cleanly to a spouse on death and is safe from a business creditor; the other goes into a court process for a year and is exposed. The difference is not the house. It is the words on the title.

Recall

Q. What is cash drag?

A. The expected return given up by holding money in safe, liquid form instead of long-term assets.

Q. What is the first thing you should do when a storm damages work on site and insurance may apply?

A. Give written notice to the insurer and the contractor within the required periods, and start contemporaneous records: dated photographs and a diary.

Q. What is an indemnity?

A. A promise by one party to cover another's specified losses or liabilities, often including claims by third parties. Its reach depends on its exact wording and is limited by caps and the governing law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Omar. Warrick's first dimension was the ownership layer. This lesson is the legal machinery inside each layer. The way an asset is held decides four outcomes: who receives it when you die, how it is treated if a relationship ends, whether a creditor can reach it, and what tax and transfer cost a move will trigger. These are concepts to help you ask the right questions. The rules differ by jurisdiction, and each point must be verified against the primary source before you rely on it.

Holding directly: sole and co-ownership

In plain English: you can own something alone, or share it, and there are two main ways to share.

Sole ownership puts title in one name. On death, the asset generally passes under the will or the rules of intestacy, usually through a court-supervised process, often called probate, before it can be transferred. Co-ownership comes in two principal forms in common-law systems. In a joint tenancy, owners hold the whole together, and on one owner's death the survivor usually takes the whole automatically by a right of survivorship, outside the will. In a tenancy in common, each owner holds a distinct share that passes under that owner's own will. Which form applies, and how it can be changed, depends on local law.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer and his business partner buy a 1,000,000-dollar site together. If they hold as joint tenants and the developer dies, the partner may take the whole site by survivorship, and the developer's family receives nothing from it, whatever his will says. If they hold as tenants in common, half passes under the developer's will. For a business asset between partners, tenancy in common is usually what partners intend; for a family home between spouses, joint tenancy is often chosen for its simplicity. The point is to choose deliberately and to check what the registered title actually says.

Say that out loud now.

Holding indirectly: company and trust

In plain English: you can own the box instead of the thing, or let someone else hold the thing for you.

When a company owns an asset, you own shares, not the asset. The company's creditors have claims on the asset; your personal creditors generally reach only your shares. On death, the shares pass, which can be simpler than transferring land, though a court process may still apply to the shares. When a trustee holds an asset, legal title sits with the trustee and the benefit with the beneficiaries; the trust deed sets the rules, and the trusts weeks will cover trustee duties properly. A nominee arrangement, in which someone holds title on your behalf with no real discretion, is a different thing again and is treated by many systems as transparent, meaning you are still the owner for most purposes.

Second worked example, hypothetical. A developer holds a 2,000,000-dollar rental building personally, and his operating company signs a contract that goes wrong, producing a 1,500,000-dollar claim. If he also personally guaranteed the contract, the claimant may pursue him, and the building is within reach. If the building had been held by a separate company from the start, with no guarantee linking it to the contract, the claimant's reach would generally stop at the operating company. Moving the building after the claim appears is a different matter: transfers made to defeat creditors can be reversed, and asset protection must happen in advance and in good faith, a topic for Week 89.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only; verify each point against primary source before you rely on it. In Canada, property and succession are mainly provincial matters, so the rules on co-ownership, probate and family property differ by province, and Quebec follows a civil law tradition with its own concepts rather than common-law joint tenancy as such. Land is generally registered under provincial systems. In Guyana, the legal system is generally described as common law in origin, with some historical Roman-Dutch influence that has been noted in land matters, and land is registered under its own national systems. In both, the questions are the same: what does the registered title say, what happens on death, what rights does a spouse have, and can a creditor reach it. The answers can differ, and a holding that works in one country may not work in the other. If you hold assets in both, you need advice in both. [unverified — confirm independently]

The four-question title review

Turn the concepts into a routine. For every asset, ask four questions and write the answers in one table. One: who is the registered or legal owner, exactly as the register or share ledger states it? Two: on my death, does this pass by my will, by survivorship, by the trust deed or by the company's articles and shareholders' agreement? Three: whose creditors can reach it, mine personally, a company's, or a trustee's? Four: what would it cost, in transfer tax, recapture and fees, to change the form? An asset whose four answers do not match your intention goes on a list for your lawyer. Most owners who run this review for the first time find at least one surprise, often a joint account or a jointly titled property that would pass differently from the will.

Family property and the relationship question

In many systems, the law gives spouses, and sometimes unmarried partners, rights to share in property built up during the relationship, whatever the title says. Holding an asset in one name or in a company does not necessarily remove it from that sharing. A domestic contract may change the position where the law allows it, with independent advice for each party. Treat this as a question to put to a lawyer, not as something a title form settles.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, in each jurisdiction where you hold assets, on title, succession and family property; accountant, on the tax cost of any change.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is holding a shared business asset as joint tenants by default, so that survivorship sends it to a partner instead of your family. The control is a title review: list each asset, read the registered title, and confirm the form matches your intention.

The beginner's mistake

Re-titling assets after a dispute or claim appears, believing it protects them. Late transfers can be reversed and can make your position worse. Structure early, for genuine reasons.

Callback

In Week 30, LEX taught ownership forms, easements and encumbrances from the buyer's side of a land deal. Today is the same title register read from the owner's side of a family balance sheet: the same words decide who takes the land when you are gone.

Recap

Sole, joint tenancy, tenancy in common, company and trust each give different outcomes on death, relationship breakdown, creditor claims and transfer. Canada and Guyana ask the same questions with different answers. Review your titles now, before anything happens.

Next: Warrick, on The Numbers: sizing the three tiers and the currency split for a hypothetical developer.
checklist: I have read the registered title of every asset I own.
I know which assets are held as joint tenants and which as tenants in common.
Shared business assets are held in the form my partners and I intend.
I know which assets would pass by will and which by survivorship.
I know which assets sit in companies and who their creditors could be.
I have taken advice in each country where I hold assets.
I never re-title an asset after a claim appears without legal advice.
head: Field checklist
speak: How an asset is legally held decides four things: who gets it when I die, how it is treated if a relationship ends, whether a creditor can reach it, and what a transfer costs. In common-law systems, sole ownership usually passes through the will and a court process. Joint tenancy usually passes to the surviving owner automatically, outside the will. Tenancy in common gives each owner a share that passes under that owner's own will. A company holds the asset, and I hold shares, so the company's creditors reach the asset and mine reach the shares. A trustee holds legal title for beneficiaries under the deed's rules. Canada and Guyana ask the same questions, though Canada's rules vary by province and Quebec is civil law, and Guyana has its own registration system, so I verify everything in each country. And I structure early: moving assets after a claim appears can be reversed.
terms: Joint tenancy — co-ownership in which the surviving owner usually takes the whole asset automatically when another owner dies.
Tenancy in common — co-ownership in which each owner holds a distinct share that passes under that owner's own will.
Probate — the court-supervised process of confirming a will and authorising the transfer of a deceased person's assets.

hostile.q: You and your partner hold the site as joint tenants. What happens to your share if you die tomorrow?
hostile.a: In many common-law systems, my partner would take the whole site by survivorship and my will would not reach it. That is not what we intend for a business asset, so we are taking legal advice on converting to a tenancy in common, or holding the site through a company with a shareholders' agreement, and checking the tax and transfer cost before we do.

title: Sizing the Three Tiers and the Currency Split, Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation for a hypothetical developer household: monthly living costs, contingent guarantees, income volatility and spending in two currencies. Step by step, it sizes tier 1, tier 2 and the currency split of each, and checks the result against the forced-sale test.
body:
A reserve sized by feel is too small in good years and too large in bad ones. A reserve sized by arithmetic answers one question: if the worst realistic month arrives, which assets do I spend, in which order and in which currency?

Recall

Q. What is the difference between joint tenancy and tenancy in common?

A. In joint tenancy, the survivor usually takes the whole automatically on another owner's death. In tenancy in common, each owner's share passes under that owner's own will.

Q. Why can a 2,000,000-dollar liquidated damages cap still leave you exposed?

A. Because it limits what you recover. If your own daily cost of delay is higher than the rate, or the delay runs past the cap, the rest is yours.

Q. What is a conditional purchase agreement?

A. A binding agreement to buy land that becomes unconditional only when stated conditions, such as financing, due diligence or approvals, are satisfied or waived.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Warrick again. On Day 1 we named the tiers; on Day 3 we priced holding them. Today we size them with numbers you can replace with your own. This is an odd week, so the calculation runs forward, from inputs to answer. All figures are hypothetical and round. The method, not the numbers, is the lesson, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Step 1: The inputs

A hypothetical developer household:

  • Living costs: 12,000 dollars a month, of which 9,000 is spent in currency A and 3,000 in currency B.
  • Income: irregular. Development fees arrive in lumps, and the household's planning assumption is that a year may pass with none.
  • Personal guarantees: a cost-overrun guarantee capped at 800,000 dollars on one project, and a completion guarantee on another whose realistic call is judged at 300,000 dollars. Both are owed in currency B.
  • Assets: 4,000,000 dollars of project equity, 500,000 dollars in a long-term portfolio, and 250,000 dollars in cash.

Step 2: Size tier 1 to living costs

Tier 1 is for spending you cannot defer. The household sets a target of 12 months of living costs, because income may pause for a year. 12 months times 12,000 dollars is 144,000 dollars. Split by currency: 9,000 times 12 is 108,000 dollars in currency A, and 3,000 times 12 is 36,000 dollars in currency B. The 12-month figure is a household choice, not a rule; a household with a salary might choose fewer months.

Step 3: Size tier 2 to the contingent calls

Guarantees are not certain, so we do not hold their full caps. We hold a realistic call. The household judges, with its advisers, that one guarantee call at a time is the realistic case, and that the larger is the cost-overrun guarantee. It estimates a realistic call of half the cap: 400,000 dollars. Add the completion guarantee's 300,000 dollars only if both projects are in construction at the same time; here they overlap for nine months, so the household holds both during that window. Tier 2 target during the overlap: 400,000 plus 300,000, which is 700,000 dollars, all in currency B, because the guarantees are owed in currency B. After the overlap, tier 2 can fall to 400,000.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Compare with what exists

Current cash is 250,000 dollars. Tier 1 needs 144,000, leaving 106,000 toward tier 2. Tier 2 needs 700,000 during the overlap, so the gap is 700,000 minus 106,000, which is 594,000 dollars. The long-term portfolio of 500,000 dollars could be counted as tier 2 only if it can be sold within the needed time at a modest cost; suppose a realistic haircut, the discount applied for selling in a stressed market, of 20 percent. Its tier 2 value is 500,000 times 0.8, which is 400,000 dollars. The remaining gap is 594,000 minus 400,000, which is 194,000 dollars.

Step 5: Apply the forced-sale test

If the 700,000-dollar double call arrived today, the household would spend 106,000 of spare cash, sell the portfolio for about 400,000 after the haircut, and still need about 194,000 from project equity. At a 25 percent forced-sale discount, raising 194,000 means selling stake worth 194,000 divided by 0.75, about 259,000 dollars at fair value, losing about 65,000. The test fails during the overlap and passes after it, when tier 2 need falls to 400,000.

Step 6: The three ways to close the gap

The household has three levers, each a decision for it and its advisers. One, raise cash before the overlap, for example from a fee due earlier or by not starting a new commitment. Two, reduce the call: negotiate a lower cap or an earlier burn-off on the cost-overrun guarantee before signing, which reduces the tier 2 target directly. Three, avoid the overlap: delay the second project's start by nine months, so only one guarantee is live at a time. The arithmetic shows that lever three alone removes 300,000 dollars of tier 2 need, more than the whole gap.

Step 6a: Price the levers

Each lever has a cost, so compare them. Raising 194,000 dollars of extra cash by not starting a side commitment might cost the fee that commitment would have earned, say 50,000 dollars. Negotiating the cost-overrun cap from 800,000 down to 600,000 might cost a slightly higher interest margin or a larger equity contribution, which the lender will price. Delaying the second project by nine months might cost carrying costs on its land, say 15,000 dollars a month, or 135,000 dollars, plus the risk that the market moves. The cheapest lever on these hypothetical numbers is the first, if the side commitment truly can wait; the most powerful is the third, because it removes a whole guarantee from the window. The household chooses with its advisers, but now it chooses between priced options instead of between worries.

Step 7: The currency check

Now test currency. Suppose currency A falls 20 percent against currency B. Tier 1 in currency A is still 108,000 units of currency A and still pays 12 months of currency A bills, so it is fine. But if any of the tier 2 reserve were held in currency A, it would now cover 20 percent less of a guarantee owed in currency B. That is why tier 2 sits in currency B. The rule from Rule 85 becomes a calculation: each tier's currency matches the obligation it serves.

Then test the opposite move. If currency B falls 20 percent against currency A, nothing in the plan breaks either: the currency B guarantees are still met by currency B reserves, and the currency A bills by currency A reserves. The pattern is the point. A reserve held in the currency of its obligation is immune to the exchange rate for that obligation, whichever way the rate moves.

Step 8: Write the answer down

TierTargetCurrencyCovers
Tier 1144,000 dollars108,000 in A, 36,000 in B12 months of living costs
Tier 2, overlap700,000 dollarsall in Bboth realistic guarantee calls
Tier 2, after overlap400,000 dollarsall in Bone realistic guarantee call
Tier 3the restas investedlong-term growth

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing tiers once and forgetting that each new project and guarantee changes them. The control is to re-run this calculation before signing any new guarantee, and every quarter.

The beginner's mistake

Counting a long-term portfolio at its full value as tier 2. Apply a realistic haircut for selling in a stressed market, because that is when you will need it.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests with base, downside and severe cases. Today is a stress test of a household: the severe case is a double guarantee call during a project overlap, and the calculation shows which lever to pull before it happens.

Recap

Size tier 1 to living costs in the currencies you spend, tier 2 to realistic contingent calls in the currencies owed, apply haircuts, run the forced-sale test, and close any gap by raising cash, reducing the call or avoiding overlap.

Next: Warrick, on The Room: the annual review meeting with a private banker who has a product to sell.
checklist: I size tier 1 to a chosen number of months of living costs, by currency.
I size tier 2 to the realistic contingent calls, in the currency they are owed.
I apply a stress haircut to any asset I count as tier 2.
I run the forced-sale test against the largest realistic call.
I check whether two guarantees will be live at the same time.
I re-run the calculation before signing any new guarantee.
I record the tier table and its date in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size my reserve in steps. First, tier 1: here a hypothetical 12 months of living costs at 12,000 dollars a month, which is 144,000, split by the currency I spend each part in. Second, tier 2: the realistic contingent calls, not the full caps. One guarantee capped at 800,000 might realistically call 400,000; a second might call 300,000; and while both projects overlap, I hold 700,000, in the currency the guarantees are owed. Third, I count what I have, applying a stress haircut to any portfolio I would sell. Fourth, I run the forced-sale test: if the double call came today, how much project equity would I sell at a discount? Here, about 259,000 dollars of fair value for 194,000 of cash. Then I close the gap: raise cash, negotiate a lower cap, or avoid overlapping guarantees. I re-run it before every new guarantee, and I confirm the plan with a licensed adviser.
terms: Haircut — a reduction applied to an asset's value to reflect what it would fetch if sold in a stressed market.
Burn-off — a provision that reduces or ends a guarantee when a milestone, such as completion or stabilisation, is reached.
Overlap — a period in which two or more projects, and their guarantees, are live at the same time.

hostile.q: You say your reserve covers your guarantees. Show me the number.
hostile.a: During the nine months both projects are in construction, my realistic guarantee calls total 700,000 dollars, owed in currency B. I hold 106,000 in spare cash and a portfolio worth about 400,000 after a stress haircut, so I am about 194,000 short in that window. I am closing it by delaying the second start until the first guarantee burns off, which removes 300,000 of need.

title: The Annual Review: When the Private Banker Has a Product to Sell
summary: A realistic scene: your annual wealth review with a private bank relationship manager who arrives with a polished proposal. How to keep the meeting about your architecture rather than their product, what to ask, what never to say, and how to leave without signing anything.
body:
The annual review is your meeting, about your plan. A relationship manager who arrives with a product is not your enemy, but he is paid by the sale. Your job is to make the plan the agenda and the product a question to be answered later, in writing.

Recall

Q. In the tier calculation, why did tier 2 sit entirely in currency B?

A. Because the guarantees it was meant to meet were owed in currency B; holding it in another currency would leave it exposed to an exchange-rate move.

Q. In the mock loss meeting, how should the meeting end?

A. With facts agreed, facts disputed, documents listed and dates set, summarised in writing the same day to all parties.

Q. What does a pre-mortem ask?

A. Imagine the project has failed badly; what most likely caused it? Then act on the answers before starting.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Warrick. As your wealth grows, you will be courted. Banks, brokers and advisers will offer to help, and many will help. Some will also sell you things you do not need, because their pay depends on it. That is not a moral judgment; it is an incentive, and Week 3 taught you to look for incentives first. This scene is about running the meeting so your architecture drives the decision. No product is recommended here, and a licensed adviser acting in your interest is required before you act.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical facts. Your annual review with Graham, a relationship manager at a private bank that holds some of your tier 1 and tier 2 reserves. You sent him your one-page architecture in advance: the three tiers, their targets, their currencies and your contingent guarantees. He arrives with a 20-page proposal for a structured investment with a higher expected yield, a five-year lock-up and early-exit penalties, and suggests funding it from your tier 2 reserve.

Opening the meeting

You speak first and set the agenda: "Thank you for coming. I want to use the time for three things: first, to confirm the reserves you hold match my tier targets; second, to talk about my guarantee overlap next year; third, if there is time, to hear your proposal. I won't decide on anything today."

That last sentence matters. It removes the pressure of a decision from the room and tells Graham you will compare whatever he says against your plan, later.

The lines to say

When he presents the proposal: "Before the yield, tell me three things. How quickly can I get the money out, and at what cost, in a bad month? Who earns what if I buy this, including the bank? And what happens to it in exactly the conditions my tier 2 is there to protect against?"

When he suggests funding it from tier 2: "Tier 2 exists to meet a guarantee call within 60 days. A five-year lock-up cannot do that job. If this belongs anywhere, it belongs in tier 3, and I would compare it with other tier 3 uses of capital."

To close the product discussion: "Please send me the full terms, the fee schedule and the exit terms in writing. I'll review them with my independent adviser."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say, "I trust you, just tell me what to do." It hands the decision to the person paid by the sale. Never say, "My reserve is just sitting there earning nothing." It invites someone to put it to work in a way that removes its purpose. Never say, "Can you get me in before the offer closes?" A deadline is a pressure tactic; a good opportunity can survive a week of review. And never reveal your reservation point on fees or terms in the first meeting.

The question behind the question

When Graham asks, "How much of your cash do you actually need?", the question behind it is how much he can move into the product. Answer with your plan: "All of tier 1 and tier 2 has a job; the targets are on the page." When he asks, "Are you happy with your returns?", the question behind it is whether you feel cash drag as a loss he can solve. Answer: "The reserve's job is protection, not return; I price the drag every year and accept it." When he says, "Most clients like you are doing this," the question behind it is whether social proof will move you. Week 3 taught you the influence principles; name them silently and move on.

When to stay silent

After you ask who earns what, stop and wait. The pause tells you a great deal: a clear, immediate answer is a good sign; a long explanation that avoids a number is not. After he finishes the pitch, do not fill the gap with enthusiasm or objection. Write down three questions and read them out.

Holding your state

A polished presentation by a confident professional creates a pull to agree. Notice it. Keep your notes on your own one-page architecture, not on his slides. Sit back rather than lean in. If you feel the pull to say yes, use the line you prepared: "I won't decide on anything today." It is easier to say a sentence you have already said once.

A second scene: the banker who is right

Run the meeting again with a different Graham. This time he says, "Looking at your page, your tier 1 is in one bank in one currency, and your tier 2 counts an undrawn credit line we could reduce in a downturn. I would not rely on that line." That is useful advice, and it may cost him business. Your lines change accordingly: "Thank you, that is exactly the kind of challenge I want. Please put it in writing, and I will take it to my adviser." The skill is not suspicion of every banker. It is judging the advice by whether it serves your architecture, and rewarding the people who tell you uncomfortable truths. Over time, you want more of the second Graham in your life, and you keep them by noticing what they did.

After the meeting

Write a short note the same day: what was confirmed about your reserves, what was proposed, the questions outstanding, and the date by which the bank will send written terms. When the terms arrive, review them with an adviser who is paid by you and not by the product. Then decide against your architecture, and record the decision and the reason in your decision journal.

Ethics and the incentive problem

The same lens applies to you. When you raise money from partners in future, you will be the one with something to sell. The standard you want from Graham, clear fees, clear exit terms, no false deadlines and a written record, is the standard you owe the people who trust you with capital. Disclose what you earn and how, before anyone asks.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is moving a protective reserve into a long lock-up because the yield is attractive and the presenter is persuasive. The control is that tier 1 and tier 2 have written jobs, and no product is bought in the meeting where it is first presented.

The beginner's mistake

Asking only about expected return. Ask about liquidity, fees, conflicts and behaviour in a crisis first; the return is the last question.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught using professionals: engagement letters, instructions and challenging advice. A relationship manager selling a product is a different relationship from an adviser you have engaged and pay. Know which one is in the room.

Recap

Set the agenda around your plan, ask about liquidity, fees and crisis behaviour before return, refuse to fund a lock-up from a protective tier, decide nothing in the room, and review written terms with your own adviser.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on wealth architecture, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I send my one-page architecture before any review meeting.
I open by setting the agenda around my plan.
I say in advance that I will not decide anything in the room.
I ask about liquidity, fees, conflicts and crisis behaviour before return.
I never fund a long lock-up from tier 1 or tier 2.
I review written terms with an adviser paid by me.
I record each decision and its reason in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: My annual review with a private banker is my meeting, about my plan. I send my one-page architecture in advance and open by setting the agenda: confirm the reserves match my tier targets, discuss next year's guarantee overlap, and only then hear any proposal. I say up front that I will not decide anything today. When a product appears, I ask three things before the yield: how quickly can I get out, and at what cost, in a bad month; who earns what, including the bank; and how it behaves in the very conditions my reserve exists for. If he suggests funding it from tier 2, I explain that tier 2 must meet a call within 60 days and a five-year lock-up cannot. I never say I trust him to decide, never complain about idle cash, and never chase a deadline. I ask for written terms and review them with an adviser I pay.
terms: Relationship manager — a bank employee who manages a client's accounts and often sells the bank's products.
Lock-up — a period during which money invested cannot be withdrawn, or only with a penalty.
Conflict of interest — a situation in which an adviser's own pay or interest could influence the advice given.

hostile.q: This offer closes on Friday and the yield is well above your cash. Why not move part of your tier 2 now?
hostile.a: Because tier 2's job is to meet a guarantee call within 60 days, and this has a five-year lock-up with exit penalties. It cannot do that job, so it does not belong in tier 2. If you send me the full terms, fees and exit conditions, I'll review it with my adviser as a possible tier 3 use of capital, and if it cannot survive a week of review, it is not for me.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 85 Review: Ownership Layers, Liquidity Tiers and Currency Reserves
summary: Six questions on the week, a recap of each lesson, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical one-page wealth plan with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom drill explaining wealth architecture to a partner.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: wealth you cannot reach, in the currency you need, when the shock arrives, does not protect you, however large it is on paper.

Recall

Q. In the annual review, what should you say before any product is presented?

A. That you will not decide anything in the meeting, and that the agenda is your plan first.

Q. What does Rule 84 require before you accept a life-safety certificate as proof?

A. That an independent reviewer with authority to stop the work has checked it against the product and system actually being built.

Q. What is the difference between an extension of time and compensation for delay?

A. An extension of time moves the completion date, protecting the contractor from liquidated damages; compensation pays the contractor's extra cost. A delay can earn one, both or neither, depending on its cause and the contract.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. This week opened the wealth phase, and it is the foundation for everything that follows: trusts, insurance, asset protection and succession all assume you know what you own, how it is held and how fast you can reach it. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three dimensions of wealth architecture?

Answer: Ownership layer, meaning the legal level an asset is held at; liquidity tier, meaning how fast and cheaply it becomes cash; and currency, meaning which currency it is worth and spent in.

Question 2. Describe the three liquidity tiers.

Answer: Tier 1 is cash available within days for living costs and immediate shocks. Tier 2 can become cash within months at modest cost, for larger shocks such as a guarantee call. Tier 3 is long-term, illiquid capital such as project equity and land. The sizes are a personal choice made with a licensed adviser.

Question 3. What was the root cause of the Thai crisis for private borrowers in 1997?

Answer: A currency mismatch funded by short-term debt: long-term assets earning baht financed by dollar loans that could be withdrawn, hidden by a peg that ended when the baht floated on 2 July 1997. Rule 85.

Question 4. How do you compare the cost of holding a reserve with the cost of not holding one?

Answer: Holding costs cash drag, the return given up each year. Not holding costs a forced-sale discount on the day a call arrives. Put both on one page and size the reserve to living costs plus realistic contingent calls.

Question 5. Why does the form of co-ownership matter for a shared business asset?

Answer: In joint tenancy, a surviving owner may take the whole by survivorship, outside your will. In tenancy in common, your share passes under your will. Partners usually intend the second; check the title and verify the local rules.

Question 6. What three things do you ask a banker before the expected return?

Answer: How quickly and at what cost you can get out in a bad month; who earns what, including the bank; and how the product behaves in the conditions your reserve exists to protect against.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Warrick framed wealth in three dimensions. Ford and Roman took the Thai baht in 1997 as a currency mismatch on short-term money, giving Rule 85. Warrick priced the reserve as cash drag against the forced-sale discount and asked you what enough means. Omar taught ownership forms and compared Canada and Guyana conceptually. Warrick sized the tiers and the currency split step by step. Warrick then ran the annual review with a private banker.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical one-page wealth plan and find the defects before reading on.

Wealth Plan, reviewed annually. Net worth: 6,000,000 dollars. Tier 1: 120,000 dollars, six months of living costs, held in the local bank in the local currency. Tier 2: our long-term portfolio of 600,000 dollars, counted at full value, plus an undrawn credit line of 500,000 dollars. Guarantees: none called to date, so excluded. Our new project site is held with my partner as joint tenants for simplicity. A higher-yield product with a three-year lock-up will be funded from tier 2 to reduce cash drag. Next review: next year.

The defects. First, guarantees are excluded because none has been called; a guarantee is a contingent liability that must size tier 2. Second, tier 1 sits entirely in one local bank and currency, which a local shock could devalue or freeze at once, contrary to Rule 85. Third, the portfolio is counted at full value with no stress haircut. Fourth, the undrawn credit line is counted as reserve without asking whether the lender can withdraw it in a stressed market, which is when it would be needed. Fifth, the business site is held as joint tenants, so survivorship could send it to the partner instead of the family. Sixth, a three-year lock-up is funded from tier 2, which exists to meet calls within months. Seventh, an annual review is too infrequent for a developer whose guarantees change with every project; review quarterly and before every new guarantee. Eighth, the plan states a net worth without an adjusted figure reflecting the forced-sale discount if the reserve is short.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new partner who asks, "You're wealthy on paper. Why are you so careful about cash?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because most of what I own is project equity that takes years to sell and sells cheaply in a hurry. I think about wealth in three dimensions. Who owns each asset, me, a company or a trust, decides who can reach it and what happens if I die. How fast it becomes cash decides whether I can pay a bill without a fire sale. And the currency decides whether a market move shrinks it. So I keep a first tier covering a year of living costs in the currency we spend, and a second tier sized to the realistic guarantee calls, in the currency they are owed. Holding that cash costs some return every year. Not holding it could force me to sell a stake at a quarter off when a guarantee is called. I price both, I re-run the numbers before every new guarantee, and I take the plan to a licensed adviser before acting."

Score your answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all three dimensions? Did you link the reserve to guarantees, not only living costs? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

Kema's rule for this drill: the partner will remember one sentence. Make sure it is the one about not being forced to sell, because that is the idea the whole phase rests on.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is confusing net worth with safety. The control is the one-page architecture with tiers, currencies, contingent calls and an adjusted net worth, reviewed quarterly.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the reserve as money waiting for a deal. A reserve with a job is not idle; it is working every day it prevents a forced sale.

Callback

In Week 63, REGA and Omar taught moving money: registration, capital controls and banking relationships. This week turned that into a household rule: keep part of your reserve outside the system you are exposed to, because the day you need it may be the day the gates close.

Recap

Wealth architecture is layer, tier and currency. Size tiers to living costs plus contingent calls, match currencies to obligations, read your titles, price drag against forced sales, and run every review on your own plan. Rule 85 keeps debt and reserves in the right currency.

head: The six questions
speak: Wealth you cannot reach, in the currency you need, when the shock arrives, does not protect you. I think in three dimensions. Ownership layer decides who can reach an asset and what happens on my death. Liquidity tier decides how fast it becomes cash: tier 1 within days for living costs, tier 2 within months for guarantee calls, tier 3 for long-term project equity. Currency decides whether a market move shrinks it, so each reserve matches the obligation it serves. Thailand in 1997 showed what happens when long-term assets are funded with short-term debt in another currency. Holding a reserve costs cash drag every year; lacking one costs a forced-sale discount on the worst day. I size the tiers to living costs plus realistic contingent calls, read every title, review quarterly and before every new guarantee, and in any banker meeting I ask about liquidity, fees and crisis behaviour before return.
terms: Wealth architecture — the deliberate design of how wealth is owned, how quickly it can be reached and in which currencies it is held.
Adjusted net worth — net worth reduced by the forced-sale discount you would suffer if contingent calls arrived without enough reserve.
Stress haircut — the discount applied to an asset's value to reflect selling it in a crisis.

hostile.q: Your plan counts an undrawn credit line as part of your reserve. Why should I believe it will be there?
hostile.a: You shouldn't, and on review I've removed it. A lender can usually reduce or withdraw an undrawn line in exactly the stressed conditions the reserve is for. My tier 2 now counts only cash and assets I can sell within the needed time after a stress haircut, and it is sized to the realistic guarantee calls.
